newsitem.title: UK: Eurostocks rebound on strong Wall St start.
newsitem.headline: Eurostocks rebound on strong Wall St start.

text.p: European bourses climbed strongly on Tuesday, boosted by Wall Street which opened with big gains after closing overnight at a near-record loss on worries about Japan's investment plans.

Stocks in Europe surged when New York roared higher by nearly one percent at the open as bargain-hunters were reassured over Japan's stance on U.S. government bonds and rushed back into the market after Monday big sell-off.

The dollar too rebounded after falling by one yen in the market turmoil which greeted Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's remarks about potential Japanese sales of U.S. government bonds. The Dow Jones industrials tumbled 2.5 percent on Monday's in its second biggest points plunge in history.

The markets turbulance was stirred when Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. government bonds and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

Before getting an extra lift from Wall Street, the European markets had already steadied after Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that Hashimoto had been incorrectly reported. "The prime minister's real intention was not reported correctly," he said.

A senior finance ministry said American government bonds were an essential investment tool in Japan's foreign reserves. Japanese purchases of U.S. bonds on a large scale has helped support Wall Street's record-breaking bull run, hence the markets dismay at talk of sales by Tokyo.

Wall Street's opening surge and the Japanese soothing words injected adrenalin into European bourses. London climbed 0.5 percent after shedding early losses of 0.8 percent and Paris climbed nearly one percent after starting down 0.5 percent.

Even before the recovery, London's blue-chip FTSE index's recent weak performance, which has seen it retreat 4.5 percent from its June 13 closing high, limited the severity of Tuesday's early markdown.
London's bond market also rebounded after the Japanese reassurances that there was no prospect of a sell-off in Treasuries which also lifted the outlook for the U.S. equities market.
"The market was talked down in the morning", one trader said. "But it was purely marked down, there was no selling pressure".
"The market is encouraging", another dealer said. "I think the downside is quite limited". But Britain's looming July 2 budget continued making investors nervous, dealers said.

Fears that the Labour government may abolish tax breaks on dividend payments for big institutional investors like pension funds has been weighing on the market in recent days, along with expectations of higher interest rates.
French stocks made the best recovery, climbing 0.9 percent at one stage in record volume thanks to huge block trades on the first day of the new account.

State-controlled French bank Credit Lyonnais was among the biggest early gainers with a 4.50 percent jump after a newspaper report that it expected a two billion franc ($343.7 million) profit for 1997 after a cost-cutting programme.

Frankfurt floor trade, which ended before Wall Street's opening, finished with only modest gains by lunch-time. After-hours dealings on the computerised IBIS index followed the rest of Europe upwards before falling back slightly in mid-afternoon.

In currency markets, the dollar rebounded to 114.80 yen by mid-afternoon from overnight lows of 114.10 when Hashimoto's remarks sent markets reeling. It was at 115.31 yen in late Europe trade on Monday.

Tokyo's reassurances have, for now, seemingly calmed currency market jitters. "We recovered pretty smartly. Hashimoto's backpedalling and the Japanese are saying all the right things," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd in New York.
The dollar also strengthened slightly against the mark, helped as the mark weakened versus the yen and hit a new 59-month low at 2.8818 versus the surging pound.
"There is still concern about the soft euro and it looks as though the trade was looking to be little bit of a buyer of dollars at lower levels," said Malpede.

Senior European policy-makers urged governments to whip their budgets into shape ahead of the euro's introduction in January 1999 but left open how much belt-tightening would actually be needed to join.

Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet said it was essential that the French government make further cuts in its 1997 budget, the critical year in which countries will be judged on their qualifications for economic and monetary union (EMU).
CURRENCIES AT 1430 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7235 marks and 114.80 yen, compared with 1.7210 and 115.31 in late European trade on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1430 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 16.8 points at 4,592.6.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 18.92 points at 2,781.82.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index finished up 1.10 points at 3755.82.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed in the afternoon at $338.35 against
$338.90 at the close on Monday. Silver was at $4.81, up two cents.
